title: Beans and Rice Feeds the World
summary: Josh and Chuck explore why beans and rice is a staple combination across the world. They cover the origins of beans in Mesoamerica, African rice cultivation in West Africa (Senegambia), the spread of rice and beans via the Atlantic slave trade to the American South, Haiti, New Orleans, Brazil, Cuba and Jamaica, and regional dishes such as feijoada, congri, moros y cristianos, rice and peas, gallo pinto, chebu jen, and Hoppin' John. They also discuss anthropologist Sydney Mintz's core-fringe-legume pattern, the nutritional case for rice and beans as a complete protein, and fiber and glycemic benefits. Personal banter and a listener mail segment about postpartum depression close the episode.
topics: New Orleans red beans and rice

segments.title: Intro and beans and rice banter
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode idea, which came from Josh's interest in why beans and rice appear across the West and islands. They chat about their favorite beans and rice styles, regional variants, and personal travel.

segments.title: Origins of beans and African rice
segments.summary: Beans were cultivated in Mesoamerica around 7000 BC; dried beans and pods are discussed, and common bean versus African pulses like pigeon peas, black-eyed peas (cowpeas), chickpeas, and lentils. Portuguese traders introduced Asian rice to Africa in the 1400s-1500s, replacing native African rice.

segments.title: Senegambia rice and Carolina rice
segments.summary: Senegambia is described as the cradle of West African rice. Enslaved people from the region were brought to plant rice in the Americas, including Carolina lowcountry rice plantations, where their knowledge was valued. Collard greens are mentioned as a Southern dish.

segments.title: Foodways of enslaved Africans and Hoppin' John
segments.summary: Enslaved West Africans spread rice and root vegetables to America. Chebu jen, a Senegalese rice and cowpea dish, is named as an ancestor of Hoppin' John, which was first printed in Sarah Rutledge's 1847 Charleston cookbook. The hosts reflect on the ethics of plantation-house dining.

segments.title: Break and mid-episode segment
segments.summary: A brief break in the episode with a sponsor or ad-break interlude before the hosts return to the discussion of rice and beans in the Americas.

segments.title: Red beans and rice in New Orleans, Brazil, Cuba and Jamaica
segments.summary: New Orleans red beans and rice traces to Haiti, where enslaved Africans cooked pigeon peas and rice (riz au pois rouge). Monday was traditional red beans and rice day from wash day. Brazil's feijoada uses cuts of pork cast off by plantation owners. Cuba's western moros y cristianos versus eastern congri reflects a Spanish divide. Jamaica's rice and peas is cooked in coconut milk with pigeon peas, allspice, and Scotch bonnet peppers. Personal anecdote about a Scotch bonnet wing.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short ad break before the final section on why beans and rice are popular.

segments.title: Core-fringe-legume pattern and global rice and bean dishes
segments.summary: Anthropologist Sydney Mintz's core, fringe, legume pattern describes basic world cuisine. Examples of other grain staples and bean dishes include Ethiopian injera, India's rajma chawal with New World ingredients, and Turkey's kuru fasulye with rice pilaf.

segments.title: Rice and beans as complete protein
segments.summary: The hosts discuss whether rice and beans form a complete protein. Amino acid content of pintos and white rice is compared, with methionine as the limiting amino acid in beans; the ratio of about 80 percent rice to 20 percent beans is mentioned as ideal when eaten in sufficient amounts.

segments.title: Personal memories and the cultural meaning of rice and beans
segments.summary: Chuck recalls a taxi driver eating rice and beans in a Cuban restaurant in New York, and Josh recalls The Grit in Athens, which served cheap rice and beans. They reflect on how the dish sustains cultures.

segments.title: Health benefits of beans and white rice
segments.summary: Beans have high fiber, with more than half a daily requirement in a cup of pinto beans, and they can lower LDL cholesterol. Beans help with glycemic index when eaten with white rice and promote satiety through hormones and slower digestion. Josh jokes about gas from refried beans.

segments.title: Closing banter and recipe request
segments.summary: Josh asks listeners to send a traditional Mexican rice recipe. Chuck and Josh joke about lard and time to prepare the dish.

segments.title: Listener mail: postpartum depression
segments.summary: Rachel from Portland, Oregon writes in to thank the hosts for their postpartum depression episode, saying it helped her feel less alone and validated her symptoms. The hosts respond.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts sign off, asking listeners to send feedback to the show email address.
